title: Exons and protein domains
takeaway: Protein domains can recur in different proteins; some exon boundaries correspond to structural or functional domains.
explanation: Gene architecture can facilitate rearrangement of segments encoding protein modules.
caution: Exons do not map one-to-one to protein domains universally.
question: Why is a one-exon–one-domain rule unsafe?
options: The correspondence varies among genes
A protein domain always spans the same number of exons
Each exon must fold into a complete independently functioning protein domain

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Compare annotated exon boundaries with protein-domain coordinates; correspondence may exist for some exons but is not a general one-to-one mapping.

title: Introns and exon shuffling
takeaway: Introns may offer noncoding regions through which recombination can rearrange coding segments.
explanation: Exon shuffling is one proposed route to new protein architectures.
caution: Do not conclude that introns exist *because* evolution designed them for exon shuffling.
question: What is defensible about exon shuffling?
options: It is an evolutionary mechanism, not an exclusive explanation for introns
Exon shuffling explains the origin of every intron
Exon rearrangement can only occur after introns are removed from the genome

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Look for homologous coding modules in different gene architectures and recombination boundaries; this supports a possible exon-shuffling history, not the purpose of all introns.

title: Gene length varies widely
takeaway: Genes vary greatly in genomic span and can contain long introns.
explanation: A protein of moderate size may be encoded by a gene that spans hundreds of thousands of DNA bases.
caution: Specific numerical 'typical gene length' depends on annotation, species and definition; the stored example is not a universal constant.
question: Why can gene span be much longer than the translated coding sequence?
options: Introns and untranslated/regulatory regions occupy genomic space
Coding sequence alone determines a gene's genomic start-to-end span
Untranslated regions contribute to span, but introns never do

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Compute genomic span from chromosome coordinates, then sum coding-sequence bases; the difference includes introns and other noncoding transcript regions.

title: How splice sites are recognized
takeaway: The spliceosome recognizes sequence and regulatory cues to define intron boundaries and exon junctions.
explanation: Splicing joins appropriate RNA exons while intronic sequences are removed.
caution: Splice-site motifs alone do not fully explain tissue-dependent isoform selection.
question: What does splice-site recognition determine?
options: Which RNA junctions are cut and joined
Which DNA chromosomes replicate
Which cell receives a signal

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Inspect the 5′ splice-site, branch-point, polypyrimidine tract and 3′ splice-site context; isoform choice also depends on RNA-binding regulators.

title: Pre-mRNA processing
takeaway: Many eukaryotic protein-coding transcripts undergo 5′ capping, 3′-end formation and splicing.
explanation: These processing steps help create export- and translation-competent mRNA.
caution: The order and coupling of processing steps are more complex than a strict linear cartoon.
question: Which set best describes typical mRNA processing?
options: 5′ capping, splicing, 3′-end cleavage/polyadenylation
DNA replication, chromosome segregation, myelination
Protein phosphorylation, glycolysis, translation

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Inspect a Pol II primary transcript for 5′ cap, spliced exon junctions, and 3′ cleavage/poly(A) tail; some modifications occur co-transcriptionally.

title: Nascent transcription
takeaway: RNA chains emerge progressively as polymerase moves along the DNA template.
explanation: Part of a transcript may be synthesized while earlier regions undergo processing.
caution: The simplified statement 'the entire gene is transcribed' does not hold for every transcript and isoform.
question: Why is a nascent transcript shorter than the final primary transcript?
options: Polymerase has not yet transcribed the entire region
Its introns have become DNA
It is a protein rather than RNA

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Nascent RNA is attached to transcription machinery and may contain incompletely synthesized downstream sequence; mature processed transcripts are different molecules/states.

title: Alternative splicing creates isoforms
takeaway: Different exon combinations or splice-site choices can yield distinct RNA isoforms from the same gene.
explanation: Two cell types may favor different isoforms of a shared gene.
caution: Different RNA isoforms do not always yield different proteins; some are noncoding or degraded.
question: What can alternative splicing change?
options: Transcript composition and sometimes protein sequence
The chromosomal copy number of the gene
The DNA bases of all cells

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Compare exon–exon junction reads and transcript models across conditions; distinct junction combinations indicate isoforms but not necessarily different proteins.

title: Exons, introns and lengths
takeaway: Typical splicing removes intronic regions and ligates exons; introns may be much longer than exons.
explanation: Large genes can produce pre-mRNAs with numerous or lengthy introns.
caution: This is a general pattern with exceptions; exon and intron definitions depend on transcript annotation.
question: What remains after canonical intron excision?
options: Joined exonic RNA segments
Canonical splicing preserves all introns while removing some exons
Canonical splicing joins introns and discards intervening exons

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Use transcript-specific exon/intron annotations; an exon can be coding or untranslated and an intron may be longer than the entire CDS.

title: Eukaryotic translation compartments
takeaway: In eukaryotic cells, most protein-coding nuclear transcription occurs in the nucleus, while translation occurs on cytosolic or ER-associated ribosomes.
explanation: Mature nuclear transcripts generally undergo export before cytoplasmic translation.
caution: Mitochondria have their own transcription/translation; not every RNA follows the cartoon.
question: Why are nuclear gene transcription and ribosomal translation spatially separated?
options: The nucleus separates nuclear DNA from many ribosomes
Protein-coding DNA is translated directly in the nucleus
All translation takes place within the nucleus before export

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Check cellular compartment: nuclear Pol II transcribes many coding genes, whereas cytoplasmic or rough-ER ribosomes translate exported mRNAs; mitochondrial genes are exceptions.

title: Eukaryotes versus prokaryotes
takeaway: Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound nuclei; bacteria lack such nuclei.
explanation: A human leukocyte is eukaryotic, while a typical bacterial cell is prokaryotic.
caution: Size alone is not a reliable definition; eukaryotes are not always larger than all bacteria.
question: What most directly distinguishes eukaryotes?
options: A membrane-bound nucleus
The presence of any linear chromosome, whether or not enclosed
Large cell size and high DNA content alone

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Ask whether a membrane-bound nucleus exists, rather than classifying an organism solely by cell size.

title: Coupled transcription and translation in bacteria
takeaway: In many bacteria, ribosomes can translate an mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
explanation: A ribosome binds a growing bacterial transcript before RNA synthesis is complete.
caution: This is a common bacterial organization, not a universal rule for all organisms.
question: What permits transcription–translation coupling in bacteria?
options: No nuclear envelope separates the processes
A bacterial nucleus temporarily opens during translation
Bacteria splice every transcript before cytoplasmic export

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Detect ribosomes bound to nascent bacterial mRNA while transcription is ongoing; compartmental separation usually prevents this for nuclear genes in eukaryotes.

title: Translation converts RNA sequence to protein
takeaway: Ribosomes interpret codons in an mRNA and assemble a polypeptide.
explanation: A coding transcript specifies amino-acid order through its reading frame.
caution: Not all RNA molecules are translated, and not every translated product remains functional.
question: What is directly decoded during translation?
options: mRNA codons
Codons in nuclear DNA directly, without an mRNA intermediate
The protein sequence itself, before new peptide bonds form

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Look for ribosomal decoding of mRNA codons into amino-acid sequence; transcription instead polymerizes RNA from a DNA template.

title: Transcription copies DNA information into RNA
takeaway: RNA polymerases synthesize RNA using a DNA template.
explanation: A cell produces a transcript of an expressed gene.
caution: Transcription makes multiple kinds of RNA; it is not restricted to mature mRNA.
question: Which enzyme catalyzes transcription?
options: RNA polymerase
Ribosome
DNA ligase

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Identify RNA polymerase copying a DNA template into RNA; distinguish the product from translated polypeptide made by ribosomes.

title: Why RNA sequencing?
takeaway: RNA-seq measures expressed transcripts instead of directly measuring DNA sequence variation.
explanation: Two cells sharing a genotype can have distinct transcriptomes.
caution: The image-only highlights cannot be checked from their text; this lesson uses the substantive RNA-seq question from the Note field.
question: You need to distinguish EGFR amplification from high EGFR transcription in GBM. Which assay combination is most informative?
options: DNA copy-number profiling for amplification plus RNA-seq for expression
Only RNA-seq, because transcript counts count DNA copies
Only H&E morphology, because morphology directly resolves EGFR amplification

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: If you need expression level or isoforms, measure RNA; if you need sequence variants or copy number, assay DNA. Neither readout directly measures enzyme activity.
optionFeedback: Correct: genomic copy number and RNA output are distinct measurements.
Incorrect: RNA expression may change without DNA gain and copy-number gain need not proportionally elevate RNA.
Incorrect: histology can characterize tissue but does not directly quantify EGFR gene copies.

title: Classical short-read RNA sequencing
takeaway: Many conventional RNA-seq workflows prepare cDNA libraries and sequence fragments, then align or quantify reads.
explanation: Transcript abundance is inferred from many short fragments rather than reading every full RNA molecule.
caution: Long-read and direct-RNA sequencing exist; this workflow is not universal.
question: Why are short-read RNA-seq counts estimates?
options: The reads represent sampled fragments of molecules
The machine captures exactly one read per cell
Sequencing directly photographs proteins

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Identify whether the library yields short cDNA-derived fragments, long native RNA reads, or another chemistry; fragment coverage biases transcript abundance estimates.

title: Mature mRNA export
takeaway: Processed nuclear mRNA is often exported to the cytoplasm for translation.
explanation: A transcript leaves the nucleus and can engage a cytoplasmic ribosome.
caution: Export is regulated; some RNAs remain nuclear and mature does not automatically mean translated.
question: Where do most cytoplasmic ribosomes translate mRNA?
options: In the cytoplasm or on rough-ER-associated ribosomes
Inside the nuclear DNA helix
Within the extracellular matrix

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: For a nuclear-encoded coding mRNA, check proper processing and export through nuclear pores; splicing alone does not guarantee translation.

title: RNA polymerase II
takeaway: RNA polymerase II transcribes most nuclear protein-coding genes in eukaryotes.
explanation: Pol II makes a primary transcript that can undergo processing.
caution: Other RNA polymerases transcribe different RNA classes.
question: Which polymerase makes most eukaryotic pre-mRNAs?
options: RNA polymerase II
DNA polymerase δ
Reverse transcriptase

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: To identify a Pol II transcription product, use a protein-coding gene or other known Pol II RNA, not a Pol I rRNA precursor or Pol III tRNA.

title: DNA base pairing
takeaway: DNA has four canonical bases and complementary pairing in a duplex: A–T and C–G.
explanation: A DNA double helix has antiparallel strands whose sequences constrain one another.
caution: Base pairing is not a complete explanation of chromatin, gene function or regulation.
question: Which DNA pair is canonical?
options: C–G
A–U in DNA
C–T

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: On an antiparallel DNA duplex, A pairs with T and C with G. RNA uses U instead of T; isolated single strands need not be paired.

title: The central dogma is a simplified map
takeaway: For protein-coding genes, DNA is transcribed into RNA and an appropriate mRNA can be translated into protein.
explanation: A coding RNA carries a sequence of codons specifying a protein.
caution: Many genes produce functional noncoding RNAs; reverse transcription also exists.
question: Which statement avoids overgeneralizing the central dogma?
options: Some RNAs function without being translated
Every functional RNA is eventually translated into a protein
Only mature mRNA can have a biological role

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Check whether the gene encodes an mRNA translated into protein versus a functional noncoding RNA. Reverse-transcribed RNA-to-DNA is a known exception to a simple cartoon.

title: Genomics vs transcriptomics vs proteomics
takeaway: DNA sequence, chromatin state, RNA abundance and protein abundance capture different aspects of molecular biology.
explanation: A tumor sample can have stable genotype but changing expression and protein levels.
caution: No single layer gives a complete readout of cell function.
question: One tumor compartment is ATAC-high at an enhancer but RNA-low for the nearby gene. What follows?
options: Accessible chromatin and transcription are distinct readouts; do not infer that the gene must be expressed
The enhancer must be bound by a specific transcription factor
The gene must produce more protein than ATAC-low cells

reference.label: Stuart & Satija, Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: DNA-seq: variant/copy calls; ATAC-seq: accessibility; RNA-seq: transcript counts; proteomics: protein abundance. These are not interchangeable outputs.
optionFeedback: Correct: accessibility, transcript abundance and protein abundance must be assessed separately.
Incorrect: an accessible site is not proof of binding by a particular transcription factor.
Incorrect: neither ATAC accessibility nor proximity guarantees protein expression.

title: DNA methylation is context-dependent
takeaway: Covalent DNA methylation can correlate with gene regulation depending on genomic location and cellular context.
explanation: Promoter methylation is one possible mechanism associated with altered transcription.
caution: Methylation does not silence every nearby gene or define protein abundance.
question: A CpG in an intragenic region is hypermethylated, while RNA expression rises. How should the result be handled?
options: Analyze the position and regulatory context rather than assuming all methylation represses genes
Discard the RNA result because methylation always silences
Assume the CpG has no function because it is not a promoter

reference.label: DNA methylation review — PubMed

decisionRule: Compare methylation at promoters, enhancers and gene bodies with measured transcription; genomic position and cellular context change the association.
optionFeedback: Correct: the relation between DNA methylation and expression varies with locus and biological setting.
Incorrect: promoter silencing is common but methylation is not uniformly repressive across genomic elements.
Incorrect: intragenic methylation can be functional; lack of promoter position is not proof of irrelevance.

title: Complementary modalities
takeaway: RNA, chromatin accessibility, proteins and imaging measure different properties of a cell or tissue.
explanation: ATAC captures accessible chromatin while spatial imaging captures morphology.
caution: ATAC accessibility does not alone prove transcription-factor binding; RNA does not measure protein directly.
question: What would ATAC-seq primarily report?
options: Accessible chromatin regions
Cell-surface protein copy number directly
Oxygen concentration

reference.label: Stuart & Satija, Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Distinguish observed accessibility peaks from measured RNA and proteins. ATAC does not prove TF binding; RNA does not directly quantify protein.

title: Gene expression is not a complete cell fingerprint
takeaway: A gene-expression profile captures observed RNA abundance and is useful for distinguishing cell types and states.
explanation: A cell's marker-gene expression supports a transcriptomic annotation.
caution: Transcriptome measurements are sparse and state-dependent; an expression profile does not uniquely identify every cell.
question: What does gene expression typically measure?
options: RNA abundance from genes
Exact DNA sequence at every locus
Direct protein activity

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Evaluate whether a cell type call is supported by multiple lineage markers, batch/ambient controls, and orthogonal identity evidence; single-cell RNA counts may drop out.

title: Genomic gene span versus coding length
takeaway: A gene's genomic span can be much larger than its protein-coding sequence because of introns and untranslated components.
explanation: A receptor with a modest protein length can be encoded by a very large gene.
caution: Numerical EGFR gene-length figures are build- and annotation-dependent and are not tested as universal facts.
question: Why is gene genomic length not equal to coding length?
options: Introns and untranslated regions contribute to its genomic span
Codons are thousands of nucleotides long
Protein length controls chromosome number

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Calculate genomic end−start span versus total CDS length from a specific transcript annotation; large introns usually explain much of the gap.

title: Splicing status is not a timestamp
takeaway: Unspliced and spliced RNA counts can inform kinetic models of transcription and processing.
explanation: RNA velocity uses relative spliced/unspliced abundances and model assumptions to estimate expression dynamics.
caution: 'Unspliced = newly made; spliced = old' is an oversimplification, not a per-molecule age measurement.
question: Two GBM cell groups have different unspliced-to-spliced ratios for a gene. Which result would justify claiming one group will differentiate into the other?
options: A longitudinal lineage or perturbation experiment supporting that transition, not the ratio alone
A larger unspliced-to-spliced ratio in the first group
A velocity arrow pointing between clusters, regardless of model fit

reference.label: La Manno et al., Nature (2018)

decisionRule: Spliced/unspliced counts can enter a kinetic RNA-velocity model, but a single splice event cannot date a molecule or prove future state transitions.
optionFeedback: Correct: kinetic RNA velocity can suggest dynamics but direct lineage or longitudinal evidence is needed for the stronger fate claim.
Incorrect: RNA processing kinetics differ among genes and populations; a ratio alone is not a demonstrated trajectory.
Incorrect: visualization of a fitted velocity vector is model-based; it does not substitute for measured transitions.

title: Introns can have regulatory roles
takeaway: Some intronic regions contain regulatory elements or affect RNA processing and gene expression.
explanation: An intronic enhancer or splicing regulator can influence expression of a gene.
caution: Not all introns have the same regulatory function.
question: Which statement is supported?
options: Some introns contain functional regulatory information
All introns are functionless once an RNA is spliced
Intronic regulation is possible only after the intron becomes protein

reference.label: Wilkinson, Charenton & Nagai, Annu Rev Biochem (2020)

decisionRule: Find conserved motifs, enhancers or splice-regulatory sequences inside introns; absence of annotation does not prove absence of function.

title: Most cells share a genome, with exceptions
takeaway: Cells in one person commonly share a germline genome but can differ in somatic variants, copy number and gene regulation.
explanation: Tumor clones acquire somatic genetic alterations, while other cells diverge in expression.
caution: The stored claim 'every cell carries the same DNA' is false as an absolute statement.
question: Which is a real exception to identical DNA across a person's cells?
options: Tumor-specific somatic mutations
A change in cytokine level alone
A change in cell shape alone

reference.label: Stuart & Satija, Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Compare tumor and matched normal DNA for somatic mutations and aneuploidy; identical germline sequence does not mean identical somatic genomes.

title: Genes and proteins: what the picture omits
takeaway: Protein-coding genes contain sequences used to produce RNA templates for protein synthesis; other genes produce noncoding RNAs.
explanation: An mRNA-encoded protein performs a cellular activity after translation.
caution: 'Every gene encodes a protein' is incorrect; the original image was not available as machine-readable explanatory content.
question: What makes a protein-coding gene special?
options: Its transcript can be translated into a polypeptide
It never contains introns
It directly contains a finished protein

reference.label: Stark et al., Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Check whether a transcript has a coding ORF and translation evidence. Many annotated genes instead produce noncoding functional RNAs.

title: Sequencing does not directly prove gene function
takeaway: DNA sequencing establishes sequence information and variants relative to reference, while functional regulation requires other evidence.
explanation: A variant can be identified by sequencing but its functional effect may remain uncertain.
caution: Original highlight overclaimed that sequencing alone identifies function and regulation.
question: What can DNA sequencing directly establish?
options: Nucleotide sequence and detectable variants
Gene function, from sequence similarity alone without validation
Gene activity in a specific tissue from genomic sequence alone

reference.label: Stuart & Satija, Nat Rev Genet (2019)

decisionRule: Sequencing detects sequence/variants; functional claims about a variant require mechanistic, expression or perturbation evidence rather than annotation alone.
